title: U.S. and Israel launch strikes on Iran
body: Reuters reported that the war began on February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Later Reuters reporting said the opening phase killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and several senior Iranian military and security figures.

title: Iran retaliates against Israel and Gulf states hosting U.S. forces
body: Reuters reported that Tehran responded to the February 28 strikes with attacks on Israel and Gulf states hosting U.S. bases. This immediately widened the conflict beyond direct U.S.–Iran and Israel–Iran exchanges.

title: IRGC official says Strait of Hormuz is closed to commercial shipping
body: An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps official said Iran had closed the Strait of Hormuz and would fire on ships attempting to pass without authorization. Reuters noted that roughly one-fifth of daily global oil consumption normally moves through the Strait.

title: Initial assessment: escalation likely remains air, missile, and maritime-centered
judgment: The conflict is likely to remain centered on airstrikes, missile/drone attacks, maritime disruption, and attacks near U.S. regional facilities rather than becoming a broad ground war. Iran is likely to use Hormuz and regional asymmetric pressure to create bargaining leverage.
probability: 60% chance the war remains primarily air/missile/maritime over the next two weeks
assumptions: The United States and Israel will avoid a ground campaign inside Iran.
Iran will prioritize regime survival and leverage over uncontrolled escalation.
Gulf states will seek to limit direct involvement while managing attacks on or near U.S. facilities.
indicatorsToWatch: Iranian statements tying Hormuz access to negotiations
calibrationNote: This assessment is plausible but incomplete. It correctly anticipates maritime leverage, but likely underestimates the later economic and shipping disruption.

title: Reuters reports major collapse in Strait of Hormuz traffic
body: Reuters reported that traffic through the Strait of Hormuz had dropped sharply since the February 28 strikes and that Iran had long prepared to restrict tanker traffic through drones, missiles, mines, and fast-boat tactics.

title: Senior Iranian political and security figures killed in continuing strikes
body: Reuters later identified multiple senior Iranian political, military, and security figures killed during March and early April, including Ali Larijani, Esmail Khatib, Ali Shamkhani, Mohammad Pakpour, and several senior commanders.

title: Tanker damage underscores continuing shipping risk
body: Reuters documented damage to the Kuwait-flagged Al-Salmi crude tanker near the Strait of Hormuz, with no injuries or oil leak reported. The incident reinforced the risk to commercial shipping even when individual attacks did not cause large casualties.

title: U.S. announces two-week bombing pause tied to reopening Hormuz
body: President Trump said he accepted a Pakistan-mediated proposal for a two-week truce and would suspend bombing if the Strait of Hormuz was opened immediately and safely. Reuters reported that the proposal was framed as a double-sided ceasefire and that Washington had received a 10-point Iranian proposal.

title: Ceasefire assessment: bombing pause likely, durable settlement unlikely
judgment: The bombing pause is likely to reduce the tempo of direct U.S.–Iran strikes in the near term, but it is unlikely to produce a rapid settlement. Iran has strong incentives to retain maritime leverage until sanctions, oil revenue, and nuclear issues are addressed.
probability: 55% chance direct U.S.–Iran strike tempo declines for two weeks; 35% chance Hormuz meaningfully reopens during that same period
assumptions: Both sides want a pause, but neither side wants to concede core bargaining leverage.
Iran views Hormuz access as a negotiation lever.
The United States faces energy-price and domestic political pressure to reduce disruption.
indicatorsToWatch: Whether Lebanon becomes part of ceasefire discussions
calibrationNote: This assessment is stronger than the March 3 assessment. It correctly treats the ceasefire as fragile and conditional, not as a durable end to the war.

title: Hormuz traffic remains far below normal after ceasefire announcement
body: Reuters graphics using Kpler data reported that Strait of Hormuz traffic remained far below prewar levels after the ceasefire announcement. Reuters also reported that the IRGC had directed ships through a route near Larak Island to avoid mines and restricted areas.

title: U.S. begins blockade of Iranian ports after talks break down
body: Reuters reported that the United States began blockading Iranian ports after talks in Islamabad broke down. CENTCOM said the blockade applied to vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports, while Iran characterized the restrictions as piracy.

title: Oil and gas disruption spills into consumer-goods supply chains
body: Reuters reported that the Iran war’s oil and gas disruption was raising costs across chemicals, plastics, packaging, and consumer goods. This broadened the issue from a regional security crisis into a global economic disruption.

title: U.S. conducts defensive strikes near Bandar Abbas and the Strait
body: A U.S. official said the United States carried out strikes on an Iranian military site, a drone control station near Bandar Abbas, and four drones near the Strait of Hormuz. The official framed the strikes as defensive and intended to maintain the ceasefire.

title: Tentative U.S.–Iran ceasefire-extension and shipping-relief deal emerges
body: Reuters reported that U.S. and Iranian officials had reached a tentative agreement to extend the ceasefire and lift shipping restrictions for 60 days while negotiators addressed Iran’s nuclear program. The report also noted that President Trump had not yet approved the deal and Iran said nothing was finalized.

title: U.S. imposes additional sanctions on Iran-linked oil trade
body: The U.S. Treasury imposed additional sanctions on vessels and entities tied to Iran’s military oil trade. The sanctions signaled that economic pressure would continue even as ceasefire and shipping-relief discussions proceeded.

title: Settlement assessment: limited deal slightly more likely than renewed major escalation
judgment: A limited ceasefire extension with some shipping relief now appears slightly more likely than a rapid return to large-scale U.S.–Iran strikes. The strongest basis is that both sides face costs from continued disruption, while the tentative 60-day framework gives each side a way to preserve leverage without fully settling the nuclear dispute.
probability: 60% limited ceasefire/shipping arrangement within 30 days; 30% continued stalemate with episodic strikes; 10% renewed large-scale direct strikes
assumptions: Energy disruption creates pressure on Washington.
Iran wants oil revenue and sanctions relief but will avoid major nuclear concessions if possible.
A temporary framework can be easier than a final settlement.
calibrationNote: This is intentionally somewhat over-optimistic. It shows realistic analytical error: provisional deal reporting can be over-weighted before implementation indicators confirm it.

title: Pentagon says U.S. is ready to restart strikes if talks fail
body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the United States was ready to restart attacks if no deal was reached. Reuters reported that President Trump would decide whether to accept the proposal for a 60-day truce extension.

title: Iran-linked media says Tehran is pausing indirect U.S. message exchanges
body: Reuters reported that Iran’s Tasnim news agency said Tehran was stopping message exchanges with Washington through mediators because of attacks on Lebanon. The same reporting said Iranian officials were discussing ways to block the Strait and activate other fronts.

title: Reuters analysis: Iran seeks limited interim deal while avoiding major nuclear concessions
body: Reuters reported that Iran favored a limited interim agreement to ease economic pressure and buy time while avoiding sensitive nuclear concessions. The report said Tehran wanted oil-revenue access, waivers, relief from the blockade, and continued leverage over the Strait.

title: Lebanon becomes more central to ceasefire diplomacy
body: Reuters reported that Israel continued strikes in southern Lebanon as the war entered its fourth month, while Iran demanded that a Lebanon ceasefire be part of a wider agreement to end the war. Lebanon and Israel held talks in Washington, but Israeli officials warned of continued action against Hezbollah.

title: Limited tanker and LNG movements suggest partial maritime openings
body: Reuters reported rare oil-product and LNG movements near the Strait of Hormuz, including tanker and LNG-carrier movements from Gulf ports. The activity suggested limited openings but not a full return to normal shipping.

title: Rubio says sanctions relief is tied to nuclear concessions, not only Strait reopening
body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told lawmakers that sanctions relief would be contingent on Iran giving up its nuclear program, not merely reopening the Strait. Reuters also reported congressional scrutiny of the administration’s war powers authority.

title: UNICEF warns war-related shipping disruption is delaying aid delivery
body: UNICEF told Reuters that Gulf shipping disruption and wider war-related transport problems were delaying delivery of lifesaving supplies, increasing costs, and forcing greater reliance on air freight.

title: Hostilities flare again as talks remain stalled
body: Reuters reported renewed Gulf hostilities, including attempted missile strikes at Kuwait and Bahrain and U.S. strikes on Qeshm Island. The same report described the conflict as stuck in a stalemate, with the Strait still largely shut and talks blocked over sanctions, nuclear activity, and maritime access.

title: Current assessment: fragile ceasefire framework, persistent flare-up risk
judgment: The conflict appears to be settling into a fragile ceasefire-and-coercion pattern rather than moving cleanly toward either durable peace or uncontrolled escalation. A limited interim deal remains possible, but renewed Gulf attacks, Lebanon linkage, unresolved nuclear demands, sanctions pressure, and Hormuz restrictions make episodic flare-ups likely.
probability: 55% continued low-to-medium-intensity conflict with periodic flare-ups over the next 30 days; 30% limited interim deal with meaningful shipping relief; 15% renewed large-scale strike cycle
assumptions: Nuclear concessions, sanctions relief, Hormuz access, and Lebanon are now linked enough that progress on only one track may not stabilize the conflict.
The United States wants sanctions/nuclear concessions before durable relief.
Israel continues to view Lebanon-related security risks as relevant to the broader war.
calibrationNote: This updates and partially corrects the May 29 assessment. The tentative-deal signal was real, but the assessment over-weighted it relative to unresolved implementation and linkage issues.
